conceptPrimer.heading: Laws of Reflection and the Deviation Angle
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Incident ray, reflected ray and the normal are coplanar, and $\angle i = \angle r$ always. A single plane mirror turns a ray through the deviation angle $\delta = \pi - 2i$: grazing incidence ($i \to 90^\circ$) barely deviates, normal incidence ($i = 0$) sends light straight back with $\delta = 180^\circ$. Micro-check: $i = 40^\circ$ gives $\delta = 180^\circ - 80^\circ = 100^\circ$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Plane-Mirror Kinematics: The $2v$ Rule
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright, laterally inverted image as far BEHIND the mirror as the object is in front. If you walk toward a stationary mirror at speed $v$, your image walks toward the mirror at $v$ too — so it approaches YOU at $2v$, while its speed relative to the MIRROR is only $v$. If the mirror itself moves, add the mirror's motion into the bookkeeping. Micro-check: walking in at $1\ \text{m/s}$, the gap between you and your image shrinks at $2\ \text{m/s}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Two Inclined Mirrors: Counting Images
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: For mirrors inclined at $\theta$, compute $m = \frac{360^\circ}{\theta}$. If $m$ is EVEN, the answer is always $N = m - 1$, wherever the object sits. If $m$ is ODD, $N = m$ unless the object lies ON the bisector, where $N = m - 1$. If $m$ is not an integer, take $N = $ the integer part of $m$. Micro-check: $\theta = 60^\circ$ gives $m = 6$ (even) so $N = 5$ images for every object position.

conceptPrimer.heading: Spherical Mirrors: Sign Convention and the Mirror Equation
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Cartesian convention: light travels $+x$, distances measured from the pole, leftward negative. Concave mirror focal length $f < 0$; convex $f > 0$; always $f = R/2$ in magnitude. The mirror equation has a PLUS sign: $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ (the lens equation carries a MINUS — do not swap them). Magnification $m = -\frac{v}{u}$. Micro-check: concave $f = -20\ \text{cm}$, object $u = -30\ \text{cm}$: $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{u} = -\tfrac{1}{20} + \tfrac{1}{30} = -\tfrac{1}{60}$, so $v = -60\ \text{cm}$, real and $m = -\tfrac{-60}{-30} = -2$ (inverted, doubled).

conceptPrimer.heading: Convex Mirrors Always Shrink
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A convex mirror gives ONLY virtual, upright, diminished images for real objects — that is why vehicles use them for a wide field of view. The focal point sits behind the mirror ($f > 0$), so the image always lands between pole and focus. Micro-check: convex $f = +20\ \text{cm}$, object $u = -20\ \text{cm}$: $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{20} = \tfrac{1}{10}$, so $v = +10\ \text{cm}$ behind the mirror and $m = -\tfrac{10}{-20} = +\tfrac{1}{2}$ — upright, half-size, virtual.

conceptPrimer.heading: Rotation, Submersion and Minimum Mirror Size
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Rotating a mirror by $\theta$ swings the reflected ray by $2\theta$ — mirrors double angles. Submerging a mirror in water changes NOTHING: reflection happens at the surface, so $f = R/2$ is untouched (unlike lenses, whose focal length depends on the medium). To see your full image in a plane mirror you need a mirror only HALF your height, positioned from head-midpoint to eye-level. Micro-check: rotate a mirror $5^\circ$ and the spot on a distant wall moves $10^\circ$.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A person walks toward a stationary plane mirror at $1.5\ \text{m/s}$. The speed of the image relative to the person is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Image and object each move at $1.5\ \text{m/s}$ toward the mirror, closing the gap at $2 \times 1.5 = 3\ \text{m/s}$.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: Two plane mirrors are inclined at $60^\circ$. The number of images of an object placed anywhere between them is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $m = \frac{360}{60} = 6$ is EVEN, so $N = m - 1 = 5$ for every object position.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: Two plane mirrors are inclined at $50^\circ$. The maximum number of images formed is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $m = \frac{360}{50} = 7.2$ is not an integer, so $N = 7$ (integer part). A non-integer answer choice is always a trap.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A ray strikes a plane mirror at incidence angle $40^\circ$. Its deviation is:
An object stands $30\ \text{cm}$ from a concave mirror of focal length $20\ \text{cm}$. The image distance from the mirror is:
An object is $20\ \text{cm}$ from a convex mirror of focal length $20\ \text{cm}$. The image is:
A spherical mirror has radius of curvature $40\ \text{cm}$. Its focal length magnitude is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $|f| = R/2 = 20\ \text{cm}$ — the focus always sits halfway to the centre of curvature.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A concave mirror is submerged in water. Its focal length:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Reflection needs no medium change, so $f = R/2$ stays put — unlike a lens, whose focal length shifts with $n_m$.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A plane mirror is rotated by $5^\circ$ about an axis in its plane. The reflected ray turns by:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Mirrors double angles: a $\theta$ rotation of the mirror swings the reflected ray by $2\theta = 10^\circ$.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The minimum height of a plane mirror in which a $180\ \text{cm}$ person can see their full image is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Half the person's height, mounted from head-midpoint down: $90\ \text{cm}$. The answer never depends on distance.

memoryHooks: Plane mirror: image as far behind as you are in front — a perfect reflection twin.
Closing speed on your own image is $2v$; its speed past the mirror is $v$.
Even $m = 360/\theta$: images $= m - 1$, wherever you hide the object.
Odd $m$: one MORE image unless the object sits on the bisector.
Mirror equation carries a PLUS; the lens equation carries a MINUS.
Concave negative, convex positive (Cartesian) — write the sign before dividing.
Convex mirrors only shrink and only virtual.
Mirrors double rotation angles: tilt $\theta$, deflect $2\theta$.
Water cannot change a mirror's focus — reflection ignores media.
commonMistakes: Using $N = m$ when $m$ is even — the correct even rule is $N = m - 1$.
Forgetting the bisector exception when $m$ is odd.
Writing $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ for mirrors (that is the LENS equation).
Dropping the minus sign in $m = -v/u$ and misreading image orientation.
Mixing up the sign of $f$: concave is negative in Cartesian convention.
Claiming water changes a mirror's focal length (it changes lenses, not mirrors).
Reporting image speed past the mirror ($v$) when the question asks speed relative to the person ($2v$).
Saying a convex mirror can form a real or enlarged image — it never can.
Rounding $m = 7.2$ up to $8$ instead of taking the integer part $7$.
examChecklist: Draw the normal first; measure $i$ from it, never from the surface.
Two-mirror counting: compute $m$ and branch even/odd/non-integer BEFORE counting.
Assign Cartesian signs ($u < 0$; concave $f < 0$) before solving the mirror equation.
Convert the solved $v$ into words: front/behind, real/virtual.
Compute $m$ with the minus and state orientation + size.
Plane-mirror kinematics: decide relative to WHOM the speed is asked.
Rotation questions: multiply by 2, then sanity-check the direction.
Immersion questions: mirror unchanged, lens changes — know which one you hold.
Minimum-mirror answers ignore object distance entirely.
Verify one ray with $\angle i = \angle r$ before trusting the diagram.
Confirm magnitudes are physical (positive distances, $|m|$ sensible).
